prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single B043 prize part naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. All six members converged on this configuration independently, but I do not treat that as evidence for the attribution. The scientific case stands on its own: an unbroken line from proglucagon processing and human incretin physiology, through identification of the biologically active truncated peptide and receptor biology, to therapies whose effects in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes are confirmed in many independent large trials. The discovery is original, mechanistically stable, mature and timely. A citation anchored in physiology and the active form keeps the prize on the discovery, and the three-person limit forces a choice that I make on that principle and not on commercial weight.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still the third slot. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide is contested against Habener and colleagues, who are not credited, and I am relying on recollection of that record, not on primary literature in the supplied material. Leaving out Knudsen can be read as ignoring the step that turned the biology into medicines, and a physiology-centred prize will be criticised as incomplete by those who weigh translation. A single GLP-1 prize also uses all three places and gives up a second part such as the unfolded protein response, which has a cleaner two-name attribution and is arguably as overdue. I accept these costs knowingly.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, moved in round 1 from Knudsen to Mojsov so that the prize rests on physiology and the active peptide, and the chair's questions ask whether Mojsov's priority is secure enough to carry a laureate place.
responses.response: I note and welcome the move, since it removes the one disagreement I took most seriously in round 1. The chair's question about evidence is the right test. What would change my position is primary-literature evidence that the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form and its insulinotropic action was established by others before or independently of Mojsov in a way that cannot be shared. A contested priority claim with a co-discoverer outside the list is not by itself that evidence, because Nobel practice has long accommodated shared credit within three names. If the committee concludes the claim fails, then Knudsen is the natural replacement, with a citation reframed around therapies, and I would not default to a different field.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that an unresolved priority dispute is a reason to scrutinise the primary literature carefully, and that he would keep Mojsov over Knudsen unless the evidence against her is stronger than the opening ballots suggest. He also asks that a Knudsen citation say plainly that it recognises translation.
responses.response: I agree with both points, and your reading of my round-1 position is accurate. Where we differ slightly is that I would put the burden of proof on the claim against Mojsov, not on her, because the published record of her work on the active peptide is not seriously doubted, only its exclusivity. I share your concern about citation honesty. If Knudsen were ever named, a citation that blurs discovery and development would be a mistake. The same standard applies to my own citation, which names the active form so that the omission of the analogue design is visible and deliberate.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks the unfolded protein response (B032, Walter and Mori) first, says GLP-1 may be almost too obvious, and asks whether a single GLP-1 prize that uses all three slots should be preferred to a split prize with B032.
responses.response: This is the strongest challenge to my configuration, and the chair's question about a two-part prize is aimed at it. I agree that Walter and Mori have the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and that the pathway is a fundamental, mature discovery. Two things keep me from splitting. First, a split would limit GLP-1 to two names and force out Holst or Drucker or Mojsov, and I do not think that is defensible for a line with this credit structure. Second, my reservation about B032 is the medical consequence criterion, since UPR modulation has no established disease-level benefit comparable to the outcome-trial evidence for GLP-1. Disease-level evidence, such as a validated intervention on the PERK or IRE1 arms with clinical benefit, would move me. I keep B032 as the leading candidate to hold for a later year, ahead of CAR-T and cGAS-STING.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius supports Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, calls recognition arguably overdue, and ranks CAR-T (B019) and cGAS-STING (B013) as alternatives because of their immunology and patient benefit.
responses.response: I agree that recognition is timely and that the safety and neuropsychiatric questions around very broad obesity use do not undercut the discovery. On CAR-T, I still think the clinical evidence is stronger than for cGAS-STING, so I keep B019 over B013, but Eshhar's chimeric-receptor concept outside the credited names means I would want a clear framing of which contribution a three-name award recognises before supporting it. For cGAS-STING I accept your point that the mechanism is robust, but I count early therapeutic translation as the reason it should wait.

responses.point: El Manira presents Knudsen and Mojsov as the two possible exclusions, says a physiology-only trio can sidestep the industrial step, and names B032 or B019 as a safer fallback if the credit record is judged too unclear.
responses.response: I agree that this is the honest framing, and I accept that a physiology-only trio sidesteps the industrial step by design. I disagree only mildly with the idea of a fallback to a different field if the credit is unclear. An unclear third slot is a reason to examine the literature and, if necessary, to swap Knudsen in, not to give up the strongest discovery on the list. I would turn to B019 or B032 only if two or more of the core names became untenable, which nothing in the supplied evidence suggests.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide is secure enough to carry a laureate place. I rely on recollection of the Habener dispute and have not verified it from supplied primary evidence.
Whether the committee prefers a physiology-centred citation or one built around therapies, which decides Knudsen versus Mojsov for the third slot.
Whether UPR (B032) will acquire disease-level evidence that would justify weighing it against GLP-1 in a later year.
Whether CAR-T can be allocated fairly without Eshhar, which governs whether B019 is a real alternative or only a nominal one.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the preferred B043 configuration or for the alternatives B019 and B032. My co-authorship of the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper and my single-cell and atlas work involve none of the credited names on those ballots. I note the chair's disclosures of co-authorship with Perlmann and Svenningsson and of Sandberg's co-authorship with me; none concerns a credited name on the shortlist. I would still recuse from any item crediting a documented co-author or former trainee.
